claim: Optogenetic techniques enable precise excitation and inhibition of firing in specified neuronal populations and artifact-free recording of firing activity.
source: Optogenetic techniques enable precise excitation and inhibition of firing in specified neuronal populations and artifact-free recording of firing activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of optogenetic techniques, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Several studies have suggested that optical stimulation provides the precision and dynamic range requisite for closed-loop neuronal control.
source: Several studies have suggested that optical stimulation provides the precision and dynamic range requisite for closed-loop neuronal control, but no approach yet permits feedback control of neuronal firing.
evidence: This claim references prior studies suggesting optical stimulation capabilities, supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: No approach yet permits feedback control of neuronal firing (as of the time of this study).
source: Several studies have suggested that optical stimulation provides the precision and dynamic range requisite for closed-loop neuronal control, but no approach yet permits feedback control of neuronal firing.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field at the time of the study, based on the authors' knowledge of existing literature.

claim: The 'optoclamp' is a feedback control technology that provides continuous, real-time adjustments of bidirectional optical stimulation to lock spiking activity at specified targets over timescales ranging from seconds to days.
source: Here we present the 'optoclamp', a feedback control technology that provides continuous, real-time adjustments of bidirectional optical stimulation in order to lock spiking activity at specified targets over timescales ranging from seconds to days.
evidence: This is a description of the technology developed in this study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The optoclamp can be used to decouple neuronal firing levels from ongoing changes in network excitability due to multi-hour periods of glutamatergic or GABAergic neurotransmission blockade in vitro.
source: We demonstrate how this system can be used to decouple neuronal firing levels from ongoing changes in network excitability due to multi-hour periods of glutamatergic or GABAergic neurotransmission blockade in vitro as well as impinging vibrissal sensory drive in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 demonstrating control during pharmacological blockade.

claim: The optoclamp can be used to decouple neuronal firing levels from impinging vibrissal sensory drive in vivo.
source: We demonstrate how this system can be used to decouple neuronal firing levels from ongoing changes in network excitability due to multi-hour periods of glutamatergic or GABAergic neurotransmission blockade in vitro as well as impinging vibrissal sensory drive in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8 demonstrating control during sensory stimulation.

claim: Feedback is essential for controlling complicated systems.
source: Feedback is essential for controlling complicated systems.
evidence: This is a general principle from control theory, representing established knowledge.

claim: Feedback can be used to define system dynamics and decouple causal interactions.
source: It can be used to define system dynamics and decouple causal interactions.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of feedback control, based on established control theory principles.

claim: A diverse set of specialized techniques that employ elements of feedback control have emerged for studying adaptation in neuronal micro-circuits.
source: Recently, a diverse set of specialized techniques that employ elements of feedback control have emerged for studying adaptation in neuronal micro-circuits (Ahrens et al., 2012), using electrical stimulation to control spike latency (Wallach et al., 2011) and firing levels (Wagenaar et al., 2005; Newman et al., 2013), improving brain-computer interfaces (Velliste et al., 2008; Cunningham et al., 2011), inducing motor plasticity (Jackson et al., 2006), and controlling intracellular firing rate (Miranda-Domínguez et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Electrical stimulation has been used to control spike latency.
source: Recently, a diverse set of specialized techniques that employ elements of feedback control have emerged for studying adaptation in neuronal micro-circuits (Ahrens et al., 2012), using electrical stimulation to control spike latency (Wallach et al., 2011) and firing levels (Wagenaar et al., 2005; Newman et al., 2013), improving brain-computer interfaces (Velliste et al., 2008; Cunningham et al., 2011), inducing motor plasticity (Jackson et al., 2006), and controlling intracellular firing rate (Miranda-Domínguez et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wallach et al., 2011.

claim: Electrical stimulation has been used to control firing levels.
source: Recently, a diverse set of specialized techniques that employ elements of feedback control have emerged for studying adaptation in neuronal micro-circuits (Ahrens et al., 2012), using electrical stimulation to control spike latency (Wallach et al., 2011) and firing levels (Wagenaar et al., 2005; Newman et al., 2013), improving brain-computer interfaces (Velliste et al., 2008; Cunningham et al., 2011), inducing motor plasticity (Jackson et al., 2006), and controlling intracellular firing rate (Miranda-Domínguez et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wagenaar et al., 2005 and Newman et al., 2013.

claim: Feedback control techniques have been used to improve brain-computer interfaces.
source: Recently, a diverse set of specialized techniques that employ elements of feedback control have emerged for studying adaptation in neuronal micro-circuits (Ahrens et al., 2012), using electrical stimulation to control spike latency (Wallach et al., 2011) and firing levels (Wagenaar et al., 2005; Newman et al., 2013), improving brain-computer interfaces (Velliste et al., 2008; Cunningham et al., 2011), inducing motor plasticity (Jackson et al., 2006), and controlling intracellular firing rate (Miranda-Domínguez et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Velliste et al., 2008 and Cunningham et al., 2011.

claim: Feedback control techniques have been used to induce motor plasticity.
source: Recently, a diverse set of specialized techniques that employ elements of feedback control have emerged for studying adaptation in neuronal micro-circuits (Ahrens et al., 2012), using electrical stimulation to control spike latency (Wallach et al., 2011) and firing levels (Wagenaar et al., 2005; Newman et al., 2013), improving brain-computer interfaces (Velliste et al., 2008; Cunningham et al., 2011), inducing motor plasticity (Jackson et al., 2006), and controlling intracellular firing rate (Miranda-Domínguez et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jackson et al., 2006.

claim: Feedback control techniques have been used to control intracellular firing rate.
source: Recently, a diverse set of specialized techniques that employ elements of feedback control have emerged for studying adaptation in neuronal micro-circuits (Ahrens et al., 2012), using electrical stimulation to control spike latency (Wallach et al., 2011) and firing levels (Wagenaar et al., 2005; Newman et al., 2013), improving brain-computer interfaces (Velliste et al., 2008; Cunningham et al., 2011), inducing motor plasticity (Jackson et al., 2006), and controlling intracellular firing rate (Miranda-Domínguez et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Miranda-Domínguez et al., 2010.

claim: True feedback control has been most broadly applied in neuroscience research using the voltage clamp.
source: True feedback control has been most broadly applied in neuroscience research using the voltage clamp, which is used to decouple the membrane potential from causally related voltage-dependent conductances.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical application of feedback control in neuroscience, based on established knowledge.

claim: The voltage clamp is used to decouple the membrane potential from causally related voltage-dependent conductances.
source: True feedback control has been most broadly applied in neuroscience research using the voltage clamp, which is used to decouple the membrane potential from causally related voltage-dependent conductances.
evidence: This is a description of the function of voltage clamp, based on established knowledge in electrophysiology.

claim: The voltage clamp approach has provided the foundation for our understanding of intracellular electrochemical signaling.
source: This approach has provided the foundation for our understanding intracellular electrochemical signaling and demands extension to other features of neural activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical impact of voltage clamp, based on established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: The neuronal firing rate is a basic feature of codes for motor action.
source: The neuronal firing rate is a basic feature of codes for motor action (Georgopoulos et al., 1988), vision (Steinmetz et al., 1987), and place (Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Georgopoulos et al., 1988.

claim: The neuronal firing rate is a basic feature of codes for vision.
source: The neuronal firing rate is a basic feature of codes for motor action (Georgopoulos et al., 1988), vision (Steinmetz et al., 1987), and place (Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Steinmetz et al., 1987.

claim: The neuronal firing rate is a basic feature of codes for place.
source: The neuronal firing rate is a basic feature of codes for motor action (Georgopoulos et al., 1988), vision (Steinmetz et al., 1987), and place (Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 1998.

claim: Changes in thalamic firing tone can alter cortical receptive fields.
source: Changes in thalamic firing tone can alter cortical receptive fields (Stoelzel et al., 2009) and the nature of temporal coding within the thalamocortical pathways (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stoelzel et al., 2009.

claim: Changes in thalamic firing tone can alter the nature of temporal coding within the thalamocortical pathways.
source: Changes in thalamic firing tone can alter cortical receptive fields (Stoelzel et al., 2009) and the nature of temporal coding within the thalamocortical pathways (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2010.

claim: Long-term changes in network firing levels can trigger a multitude of homeostatic processes that regulate circuit excitability and stability.
source: Long-term changes in network firing levels can trigger a multitude of homeostatic processes that regulate circuit excitability and stability (Turrigiano et al., 1998; Corner et al., 2002; Turrigiano, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Turrigiano et al., 1998; Corner et al., 2002; and Turrigiano, 2011.

claim: Optogenetic tools are routinely used to provide genetically specified, millisecond time-scale stimulation or suppression of neural activity with light during simultaneous, artifact-free electrical recording.
source: Optogenetic tools are routinely used to provide genetically specified, millisecond time-scale stimulation or suppression of neural activity with light (Mattis et al., 2011) during simultaneous, artifact-free electrical recording.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mattis et al., 2011 and represents established knowledge about optogenetic tools.

claim: Several studies have presented closed-loop optogenetic stimulation techniques.
source: Although several studies have presented closed-loop optogenetic stimulation techniques (Leifer et al., 2011; Stirman et al., 2011; Paz et al., 2012; Krook-Magnuson et al., 2013; O'Connor et al., 2013; Siegle and Wilson, 2014), no approach yet permits feedback control of neuronal firing levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: No approach yet permits feedback control of neuronal firing levels (prior to this study).
source: Although several studies have presented closed-loop optogenetic stimulation techniques (Leifer et al., 2011; Stirman et al., 2011; Paz et al., 2012; Krook-Magnuson et al., 2013; O'Connor et al., 2013; Siegle and Wilson, 2014), no approach yet permits feedback control of neuronal firing levels.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study, based on the authors' knowledge of existing literature.

claim: The optoclamp allows precise control of population firing levels in dissociated cortical networks over timescales ranging from seconds to days.
source: We show that the optoclamp allows precise control of population firing levels in dissociated cortical networks over timescales ranging from seconds to days.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2-6.

claim: Firing rate control can be achieved over many hours and used to restore pre-drug firing levels during chronic blockade of excitatory or inhibitory synaptic transmission.
source: We show that firing rate control can be achieved over many hours and used to restore pre-drug firing levels during chronic blockade of excitatory or inhibitory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Changes in firing levels are not required to induce homeostatic alterations in network excitability.
source: Using this approach, we decouple the effects of suppressed neurotransmission from the indirect effects on network firing, and find that changes in firing levels are not required to induce homeostatic alterations in network excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6, where homeostatic changes occurred despite clamped firing rates.

claim: Background thalamic activity levels can be controlled during ongoing sensory input without corrupting the fine-scale temporal structure of whisker-evoked spike trains.
source: We find that background thalamic activity levels can be controlled during ongoing sensory input without corrupting the fine-scale temporal structure of whisker-evoked spike trains.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Evoked population firing rates were positively correlated with UC (the excitatory control variable).
source: Evoked population firing rates were positively correlated with UC and negatively correlated with UH (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Evoked population firing rates were negatively correlated with UH (the inhibitory control variable).
source: Evoked population firing rates were positively correlated with UC and negatively correlated with UH (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: UC-evoked firing levels saturated at approximately 12.5 Hz/unit corresponding to UC = 0.47.
source: UC-evoked firing levels saturated at approximately 12.5 Hz/unit corresponding to UC = 0.47 (freq. = 14.7 Hz, pulse-width: 2.4 ms, power at 465 nm: 6.9 mW·mm−2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Firing rate suppression saturated at 0.04 Hz/unit corresponding to UH = 0.15.
source: Firing rate suppression saturated at 0.04 Hz/unit corresponding to UH = 0.15 (power at 590 nm: 1.8 mW mm−2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The monotonic relationships between UC and UH and network firing levels indicated their applicability as closed-loop control signals.
source: The monotonic relationships between UC and UH and network firing levels indicated their applicability as closed-loop control signals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing monotonic relationships in Figure 1B.

claim: Synaptic blockade strongly affected mean spontaneous firing levels (CNQX: −74.2%, AP5: −66.6%, bicuculine: +357%).
source: Synaptic blockade strongly affected mean spontaneous firing levels (CNQX: −74.2%, AP5: −66.6%, bicuculine: +357%) and network-level signal propagation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Firing in CNQX-treated networks could be driven over the same dynamic range as the drug free condition (0.057 to 13.3 Hz/unit).
source: In spite of this, firing in CNQX- and AP5-treated networks could be driven over the same dynamic range as the drug free condition (Figure 1B; CNQX: 0.057 to 13.3 Hz/unit, AP5: 0.088 to 12.6 Hz/unit), indicating that optogenetic input could compensate for depressed excitatory transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Firing in AP5-treated networks could be driven over the same dynamic range as the drug free condition (0.088 to 12.6 Hz/unit).
source: In spite of this, firing in CNQX- and AP5-treated networks could be driven over the same dynamic range as the drug free condition (Figure 1B; CNQX: 0.057 to 13.3 Hz/unit, AP5: 0.088 to 12.6 Hz/unit), indicating that optogenetic input could compensate for depressed excitatory transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Optogenetic input could compensate for depressed excitatory transmission.
source: In spite of this, firing in CNQX- and AP5-treated networks could be driven over the same dynamic range as the drug free condition (Figure 1B; CNQX: 0.057 to 13.3 Hz/unit, AP5: 0.088 to 12.6 Hz/unit), indicating that optogenetic input could compensate for depressed excitatory transmission.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing that firing could be driven to similar levels despite synaptic blockade.

claim: Bicuculline greatly reduced the dynamic range of evoked network activity (0.095 to 5.1 Hz/unit), indicating a loss of reliable activity modulation.
source: Bicuculline greatly reduced the dynamic range of evoked network activity indicating a loss of reliable activity modulation (Figure 1B; 0.095 to 5.1 Hz/unit).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Open-loop stimuli lost effectiveness throughout each 60-s trial causing significant second-to-second drift in evoked activity levels.
source: Although time-averaged firing levels were monotonically related to UC and UH (Figure 1B), open-loop stimuli lost effectiveness throughout each 60-s trial causing significant second-to-second drift in evoked activity levels (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Decreases in stimulus efficacy using ChR2R were likely due to network adaptation, rather than changes in ChR2R-mediated photocurrents.
source: Decreases in stimulus efficacy using ChR2R were likely due to network adaptation, rather than changes in ChR2R-mediated photocurrents (Mattis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by citation to Mattis et al., 2011.

claim: Decreased efficacy of eNpHR3.0-mediated firing suppression likely resulted from a loss of synaptic inhibition due to intracellular Cl− accumulation and decreased outward photocurrents due to pump desensitization.
source: Aside from network adaptation, deceased efficacy of eNpHR3.0-mediated firing suppression likely resulted from a loss of synaptic inhibition due to intracellular Cl− accumulation (Raimondo et al., 2012) and decreased outward photocurrents due to pump desensitization (Mattis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by citations to Raimondo et al., 2012 and Mattis et al., 2011.

claim: Successful control was achieved in over 90% of trials (71/77 trials) with mean RMS tracking error 0.14 ± 0.091 Hz/unit.
source: We tested the controller using 60-s, randomly-ordered targets ranging from 0–10 Hz/unit (Figure 2A; 7 cultures, 11 trials/culture), and successful control was achieved in over 90% of trials (Figure 2B; 71/77 trials; mean RMS tracking error 0.14 ± 0.091 Hz/unit).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Tracking error increased with target rate.
source: Tracking error increased with target rate, and occasionally the stimulator saturated before the trial was complete (e.g., Figure 2A, grey line).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Control settling time varied across preparations and was not correlated with the target firing rate (mean ± SD, 7.83 ± 6.07 s).
source: Control settling time varied across preparations and was not correlated with the target firing rate (mean ± SD, 7.83 ± 6.07 s; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The controller was capable of tracking continuously varying targets.
source: Although we generally used discrete steps in the target firing rate, the controller was also capable of tracking continuously varying targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Functional control was achieved at K < 1.0, 1.0 s < Ti <10 s, and 0.5 s <τ <10 s.
source: Functional control was achieved at K < 1.0, 1.0 s < Ti <10 s, and 0.5 s <τ <10 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 through Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Outside of the functional parameter bounds, closed-loop dynamics were unstable and/or firing levels exhibited significant target offsets.
source: Outside of these bounds, closed-loop dynamics were unstable and/or firing levels exhibited significant target offsets (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 through Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 through Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The control signals, UC and UH, were highly variable across networks, even for the same target rate.
source: The control signals, UC and UH, were highly variable across networks, even for the same target rate (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Variability in control signals likely reflects heterogeneous network excitability, opsin expression, synaptic connectivity, and developmental processes.
source: This variability likely reflects heterogeneous network excitability, opsin expression, synaptic connectivity, and developmental processes (Wagenaar et al., 2006) and suggests that the controller continuously adapts to ongoing changes in network excitability in order to precisely clamp firing levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed variability and supported by citation to Wagenaar et al., 2006.

claim: Open-loop replay of successful closed-loop control signals were incapable of controlling firing.
source: To test this possibility, we delivered open-loop replay of successful closed-loop control signals and found they were incapable of controlling firing (Figure 4, Figure 2 cultures).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Real-time feedback is necessary to achieve precise control of neural firing, even for same target rate within single preparations.
source: This demonstrates the necessity of real-time feedback to achieve precise control of neural firing, even for same target rate within single preparations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the open-loop replay experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Control performance during AMPAergic and NMDAergic transmission blockade was equivalent to the drug-free case.
source: Next, we used the PI controller to clamp network firing levels to targets between 0 and 10 Hz/unit during blockade of AMPAergic and NMDAergic transmission (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A; 'Materials and methods'). Control performance was equivalent to the drug-free case and control failure was isolated to high target rates (9–10 Hz/unit) due to stimulus saturation (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Control failure during AMPAergic and NMDAergic transmission blockade was isolated to high target rates (9–10 Hz/unit) due to stimulus saturation.
source: Control performance was equivalent to the drug-free case and control failure was isolated to high target rates (9–10 Hz/unit) due to stimulus saturation (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Reliable control was not possible during blockade of GABAergic transmission.
source: We also tested PI control during blockade of GABAergic transmission and found that reliable control was not possible (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The inability to control during GABAergic blockade is likely due to the destabilizing effects of bicuculline, which caused the controller to oscillate.
source: This is likely due to the destabilizing effects of bicuculline, which caused the controller to oscillate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed control failure during bicuculline treatment.

claim: The result of control failure during GABAergic blockade is consistent with studies indicating a general role of reduced inhibition in diseases of circuit instability such as temporal lobe epilepsy and Dravet syndrome.
source: This result is consistent with studies indicating a general role of reduced inhibition in diseases of circuit instability such as temporal lobe epilepsy (Kobayashi and Buckmaster, 2003) and Dravet syndrome (Dutton et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kobayashi and Buckmaster, 2003 and Dutton et al., 2013.

claim: The controller made rapid, second-to-second adjustments in stimulus intensity to maintain the instantaneous target rate during 5-min control epochs.
source: During each 5-min step, the controller made rapid, second-to-second adjustments in stimulus intensity to maintain the instantaneous target rate, while slower changes in stimulus intensity occurred over minutes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Slower changes in stimulus intensity occurred over minutes during extended control periods.
source: During each 5-min step, the controller made rapid, second-to-second adjustments in stimulus intensity to maintain the instantaneous target rate, while slower changes in stimulus intensity occurred over minutes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Minute-to-minute changes in the control signal intensity likely reflect short-term synaptic depression and changes in cellular excitability that accrued over each control epoch.
source: Minute-to-minute changes in the control signal intensity likely reflect short-term synaptic depression and changes in cellular excitability that accrued over each control epoch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in control signals over time.

claim: The control signal can be used as a readout of network excitability, analogous to how injected current from a voltage clamp amplifier can be used to assess cellular excitability.
source: Therefore, the control signal can be used as a readout of network excitability, analogous to how injected current from a voltage clamp amplifier can be used to asses cellular excitability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that control signals reflect network excitability changes.

claim: Different stimulus waveforms (triangular, sinusoidal, PRBS, and direct intensity modulation) all permitted successful closed-loop control.
source: To test how different stimulus waveforms affected network response correlations during PI control, we mapped UC onto triangular, sinusoidal, pseudorandom binary sequence (PRBS), and direct intensity modulation inputs (Tchumatchenko et al., 2013). Each permitted successful closed-loop control, but notably, the choice of stimulus waveform significantly affected the peak firing correlation (P = 6.5 × 10−24) and synchrony (P = 10−22) of the population response (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The choice of stimulus waveform significantly affected the peak firing correlation (P = 6.5 × 10−24) and synchrony (P = 10−22) of the population response.
source: Each permitted successful closed-loop control, but notably, the choice of stimulus waveform significantly affected the peak firing correlation (P = 6.5 × 10−24) and synchrony (P = 10−22) of the population response (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Square pulse trains typically used for ChR2-based stimulation resulted in periodic, highly correlated population firing.
source: The square pulse trains typically used for ChR2-based stimulation (Mattis et al., 2011) resulted in periodic, highly correlated population firing (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and citation to Mattis et al., 2011.

claim: Compared to square pulses, sinusoidal stimuli decreased peak unit-to-unit firing correlations (−10.6%, p = 0.028), but did not affect synchrony.
source: Compared to square pulses, sinusoidal stimuli decreased peak unit-to-unit firing correlations (−10.6%, p = 0.028), but did not affect synchrony.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4.

claim: PRBS stimuli reduced peak correlations (−24.0%, p = 6.8 × 10−13) and firing synchrony (−17.9%, p = 4.6 × 10−8).
source: PRBS stimuli reduced peak correlations (−24.0%, p = 6.8 × 10−13) and firing synchrony (−17.9%, p = 4.6 × 10−8).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Continuous light modulation increased both correlations (+21.3%, p = 4.3 × 10−5) and synchrony (+41.4%, p = 2.5 × 10−9).
source: Continuous light modulation increased both correlations (+21.3%, p = 4.3 × 10−5) and synchrony (+41.4%, p = 2.5 × 10−9).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Triangular pulses did not affect correlation or synchrony.
source: Triangular pulses did not affect correlation or synchrony.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Periodic input signals produced a periodic response, while PBRS input and continuous intensity modulation resulted in non-periodic firing.
source: Importantly, while periodic input signals produced a periodic response, PBRS input and continuous intensity modulation resulted in non-periodic firing.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In its current form, the optoclamp only controls population firing levels and leaves more complex features of neural activity unconstrained and subject to the influence of network connectivity, network dynamics, and the nature of the stimulus signal.
source: This emphasizes the fact that, in its current form, the optoclamp only controls population firing levels and leaves more complex features of neural activity unconstrained and subject to the influence of network connectivity, network dynamics, and the nature of the stimulus signal.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that different stimulus waveforms produce different higher-order statistics.

claim: The on-off controller successfully held firing rates at six of seven targets over 12-hr epochs, saturating only at 6 Hz/unit after ∼7 hr.
source: We tested on-off control by clamping network firing rates within a single culture to seven elevated setpoints (ranging from 0.75 to 6 Hz/unit) for 12-hr epochs (Figure 5). The on-off controller successfully held firing rates at six of these targets, saturating only at 6 Hz/unit after ∼7 hr (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The stimulation frequency required to maintain each target firing rate was better correlated to the difference between the target and the pre-clamp firing rate than the target rate alone (R2 = 0.63 vs 0.52).
source: Notably, the stimulation frequency required to maintain each target firing rate was better correlated to the difference between the target and the pre-clamp firing rate than the target rate alone (R2 = 0.63 vs 0.52; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Alterations in network excitability across different experimental days were reflected in the intensity of the control inputs.
source: This indicates that alterations in network excitability across different experimental days were reflected in the intensity of the control inputs (Figure 5C,D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and suggests that optogenetic feedback control can be used to study changes in neuronal network dynamics over developmental timescales.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between control inputs and pre-clamp firing rates.

claim: Optogenetic feedback control can be used to study changes in neuronal network dynamics over developmental timescales.
source: This indicates that alterations in network excitability across different experimental days were reflected in the intensity of the control inputs (Figure 5C,D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and suggests that optogenetic feedback control can be used to study changes in neuronal network dynamics over developmental timescales.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications based on the observed results.

claim: Both excitatory and inhibitory on-off control were better able to preserve spontaneous activity correlations than PI control.
source: We found that both excitatory and inhibitory on-off control were better able to preserve spontaneous activity correlations than PI control (Figure 5E; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: For targets that required higher excitatory stimulation rates during on-off control, a periodic correlation structure emerged.
source: However, for targets that required higher excitatory stimulation rates during on-off control, a periodic correlation structure emerged (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Previous in vitro studies have shown that chronic elevation in network activity using GABAergic transmission blockers leads to a homeostatic reduction in firing rate following relief from blockade.
source: Previous in vitro studies have shown that chronic elevation in network activity using GABAergic transmission blockers leads to a homeostatic reduction in firing rate following relief from blockade (Turrigiano et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Turrigiano et al., 1998.

claim: Chronic reductions in activity using glutamatergic blockers elicit homeostatic increases in firing rate.
source: Conversely, chronic reductions in activity using glutamatergic blockers elicit homeostatic increases in firing rate (Corner et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Corner et al., 2002.

claim: Homeostatic changes in firing rate were not observed following prolonged increases or decreases in network spiking activity during on-off feedback control.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe homeostatic changes in firing rate following prolonged increases or decreases in network spiking activity during on-off feedback control (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Altered synaptic transmission and altered spiking activity may have distinct effects on homeostatic regulation of network excitability.
source: This suggests that altered synaptic transmission and altered spiking activity may have distinct effects on homeostatic regulation of network excitability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that homeostatic changes did not occur when firing was clamped.

claim: The controller effectively clamped firing rates to pre-drug levels during CNQX, AP5, or bicuculline treatment.
source: We treated networks with CNQX (2 cultures), AP5 (2 cultures), or bicuculline (1 culture), and then used on-off control to restore pre-drug firing rates during 24-hr (CNQX or AP5) or 3-hr (bicuculline) periods. In all cases, the controller effectively clamped firing rates to pre-drug levels (Figure 6A.v,B.v,C.v).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.v, B.v, and C.v.

claim: Application of CNQX or AP5 caused marked reductions in network spiking activity compared to the pre-drug levels and these reduced activity levels were sustained upon relief from on-off control.
source: As expected, application of CNQX or AP5 caused marked reductions in network spiking activity compared to the pre-drug levels and these reduced activity levels were sustained upon relief from on-off control (Figure 6A.v,B.v).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.v and B.v.

claim: Bicuculline greatly increased firing rate, both before and after the clamp period.
source: Meanwhile, bicuculline greatly increased firing rate, both before and after the clamp period (Figure 6C.v).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.v.

claim: Following drug removal after CNQX treatment, spontaneous firing was elevated compared to pre-drug levels (CNQX: +86.4 and +21.1%).
source: Following drug removal, spontaneous firing was elevated compared to pre-drug levels (CNQX: +86.4 and +21.1%, AP5: +157.4 and +273.3%).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.v.

claim: Following drug removal after AP5 treatment, spontaneous firing was elevated compared to pre-drug levels (AP5: +157.4 and +273.3%).
source: Following drug removal, spontaneous firing was elevated compared to pre-drug levels (CNQX: +86.4 and +21.1%, AP5: +157.4 and +273.3%).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.v.

claim: After washing bicuculline, firing was reduced by 47.2% compared to pre-drug levels.
source: After washing bicuculline, firing was reduced by 47.2% compared to pre-drug levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.v.

claim: Homeostatic changes in spiking levels were observed following prolonged glutamatergic or GABAergic blockade even though network firing rates were maintained at pre-drug levels during the treatment windows.
source: Notably, homeostatic changes in spiking levels were observed following prolonged glutamatergic or GABAergic blockade even though network firing rates were maintained at pre-drug levels during the treatment windows.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Changes in firing rate were not required to drive compensatory alterations in network excitability.
source: This indicates that changes in firing rate were not required to drive compensatory alterations in network excitability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that homeostatic changes occurred despite clamped firing rates.

claim: Homeostatic alterations of network excitability were triggered directly by suppressed synaptic activity.
source: Instead, homeostatic alterations of network excitability were triggered directly by suppressed synaptic activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that homeostatic changes occurred despite clamped firing rates.

claim: On-off control has recently been used to show that upward synaptic scaling is directly induced via reductions in AMPA receptor activation.
source: In line with this result, on-off control has recently been used to show that upward synaptic scaling, the most widely studied form of homeostatic plasticity, is directly induced via reductions in AMPA receptor activation (Fong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fong et al., 2015.

claim: For > 75% of TCUs, the controller effectively clamped firing over a range of target rates, which varied across cells.
source: We used optogenetic feedback to clamp firing rates in TCUs at increasing target levels for 30-s epochs (Figure 7B). For > 75% of TCUs, the controller effectively clamped firing over a range of target rates, which varied across cells (e.g., 4–40 Hz vs 18–22 Hz; Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The RMS tracking error for in vivo control was larger than for in vitro control (mean ± SD, 2.0 ± 0.8 Hz).
source: Because firing rate estimates were derived from single cells instead of population activity, the RMS tracking error was larger than for in vitro control (mean ± SD, 2.0 ± 0.8 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Controller settling time for in vivo control was not correlated to the target firing rate and was shorter than for in vitro control (mean ± SD, 3.3 ± 3.2 s).
source: Controller settling time was not correlated to the target firing rate and was shorter than for in vitro control (mean ± SD, 3.3 ± 3.2 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the in vivo experiments.

claim: The optical power required for successful control varied greatly from cell to cell.
source: The optical power required for successful control varied greatly from cell to cell (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The mean optical intensity required for successful control at 16 Hz spanned nearly two orders of magnitude (0.66–22.92 mW mm−2).
source: For instance, the mean optical intensity required for successful control at 16 Hz, the most widely achieved target in our sample, spanned nearly two orders of magnitude (0.66–22.92 mW mm−2; Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Open-loop optical stimuli would not result in consistent firing rates.
source: This suggests that open-loop optical stimuli would not result in consistent firing rates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of high variability in required optical power.

claim: Linear increases in optical intensity resulted in extremely variable and temporally non-stationary firing over trials and units.
source: Indeed, we found that linear increases in optical intensity resulted in extremely variable and temporally non-stationary firing over trials and units (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Locking optical power at the mid-trial or trial-averaged level significantly increased RMS tracking error (+204 ± 227% and +238 ± 145%, respectively, p < 10−14 for both).
source: Locking optical power at the mid-trial or trial-averaged level significantly increased RMS tracking error (+204 ± 227% and +238 ± 145%, respectively, p < 10−14 for both).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Continuous stimulus updates are required to exert precise control over neural activity in vivo.
source: This indicates that continuous stimulus updates are required to exert precise control over neural activity in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control locking experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increasing τ (from 0.8 to 1.6 s) introduced lag into the control loop, causing overshoot, decreased stability, and a significant increase in RMS tracking error (+57%, p = 1.4 × 10−6).
source: Increasing τ (from 0.8 to 1.6 s) introduced lag into the control loop, causing overshoot, decreased stability, and a significant increase in RMS tracking error (+57%, p = 1.4 × 10−6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lowering τ (from 0.8 to 0.16 s) decreased overshoot and significantly reduced RMS tracking error (−46.9%, p = 1.2 × 10−10).
source: Conversely, lowering τ (from 0.8 to 0.16 s) decreased overshoot and significantly reduced RMS tracking error (−46.9%, p = 1.2 × 10−10).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Increasing Ti (from 1 to 10 s) did not significantly affect RMS tracking error (p = 0.088), but caused over-damping and increased controller settling time.
source: Increasing Ti (from 1 to 10 s) did not significantly affect RMS tracking error (p = 0.088), but caused over-damping and increased controller settling time.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Reducing Ti (from 1 to 0.1 s) significantly decreased RMS tracking error (−18%, p = 0.011) and introduced overshoot during control onset.
source: Reducing Ti (from 1 to 0.1 s) significantly decreased RMS tracking error (−18%, p = 0.011) and introduced overshoot during control onset.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Low-latency feedback and a short integral time constant improve the performance of firing rate control in vivo.
source: Together, these results indicate that low-latency feedback and a short integral time constant improve the performance of firing rate control in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the parameter sweep experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the in vivo experiment, τ = 0.16 s and Ti = 1 s gave the best performance in terms of RMS error.
source: In this experiment, τ = 0.16 s and Ti = 1 s gave the best performance in terms of RMS error.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the parameter sweep experiments.

claim: In the awake animal, sensory thalamic spike trains tend to exhibit irregular firing with interval statistics close to those of a Poisson process.
source: In the awake animal, sensory thalamic spike trains tend to exhibit irregular firing with interval statistics close to those of a Poisson process (Poggio and Viernstein, 1964).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Poggio and Viernstein, 1964.

claim: Drugs used for anesthesia have profound effects on evoked and background firing, receptive field properties, and subthreshold voltage statistics in the vibrissal pathway.
source: Drugs used for anesthesia have profound effects on evoked and background firing (Simons et al., 1992), receptive field properties (Friedberg et al., 1999), and subthreshold voltage statistics (Constantinople and Bruno, 2011) in the vibrissal pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Simons et al., 1992; Friedberg et al., 1999; and Constantinople and Bruno, 2011.

claim: Across target rates and units, CVISI was close to 1, indicating a Poisson-like spiking process (mean ± SD, 1.31 ± 0.33).
source: Across target rates and units, we found a CVISI close to 1, indicating a Poisson-like spiking process (mean ± SD, 1.31 ± 0.33 across targets and units; Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The CVISI of spontaneous unit activity was significantly elevated (mean ± SD, 1.72 ± 0.43; p = 0.043), likely due to an increased propensity for burst firing in sensory thalamus during anesthesia and non-alert states.
source: In comparison, the CVISI of spontaneous unit activity was significantly elevated (Figure 7F, inset) mean ± SD, 1.72 ± 0.43; p = 0.043), likely due to an increased propensity for burst firing in sensory thalamus during anesthesia and non-alert states (Stoelzel et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7F and citation to Stoelzel et al., 2009.

claim: Optogenetic feedback control using continuously modulated input can be used to mimic alert, Poisson-like spiking statistics in anesthetized animals.
source: This suggests that optogenetic feedback control using continuously modulated input can be used to mimic alert, Poisson-like spiking statistics in anesthetized animals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that controlled firing had lower CVISI than spontaneous firing.

claim: Vibrissa deflections evoked stimulus-locked spike trains both in the presence and absence of closed-loop control.
source: Finally, we tested whether the controller could clamp firing during ongoing sensory drive. We recorded from TCUs that were responsive to punctate deflections of the corresponding primary vibrissa (5 TCUs, 8° at ∼1600 deg. s−1, 10 Hz; Figure 8—figure supplement 1; 'Materials and methods'). Vibrissa deflections evoked stimulus-locked spike trains both in the presence and absence of closed-loop control (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Whisker stimuli resulted in little or no performance degradation of firing rate control in terms of mean TCU firing rate (p = 0.09) or RMS tracking error (p = 0.73) compared to control without whisker input.
source: However, whisker stimuli resulted in little or no performance degradation of firing rate control in terms of mean TCU firing rate (Figure 8B; p = 0.09) or RMS tracking error (Figure 8C; p = 0.73) compared to control without whisker input.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: To maintain control during sensory stimulation, the controller automatically decreased LED stimulus intensity to accommodate sensory drive (mean ± SD, 8.4 ± 5.34 to 4.9 ± 4.8 mW mm−2, p = 0.024).
source: To maintain control during sensory stimulation, the controller automatically decreased LED stimulus intensity to accommodate sensory drive (Figure 8D; mean ± SD, 8.4 ± 5.34 to 4.9 ± 4.8 mW mm−2, p = 0.024).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: During concurrent whisker stimulation and closed-loop control, the FWHM of the STA for optical power and whisker position differed by more than an order of magnitude (mean ± SD FWHM of STA: optical power, 0.46 ± 0.2 s vs whisker position, 18.3 ± 5.5 ms, p = 0.0079).
source: To characterize the timescales over which the optical controller and whisker stimuli affected firing, we calculated the spike-triggered average (STA) of optical power and whisker position (Figure 8E,F). During concurrent whisker stimulation and closed-loop control, the full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) of the STA for optical power and whisker position differed by more than an order of magnitude, indicating that sensory input and optical control signals affected firing on distinct timescales (Figure 8G; mean ± SD FWHM of STA: optical power, 0.46 ± 0.2 s vs whisker position, 18.3 ± 5.5 ms, p = 0.0079).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8E, F, and G.

claim: Sensory input and optical control signals affected firing on distinct timescales.
source: During concurrent whisker stimulation and closed-loop control, the full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) of the STA for optical power and whisker position differed by more than an order of magnitude, indicating that sensory input and optical control signals affected firing on distinct timescales (Figure 8G; mean ± SD FWHM of STA: optical power, 0.46 ± 0.2 s vs whisker position, 18.3 ± 5.5 ms, p = 0.0079).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the STA analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Optogenetic feedback control using continuously modulated input provides a means to control baseline firing state without distorting the fine-scale temporal structure of sensory-evoked spike trains.
source: Therefore, optogenetic feedback control using continuously modulated input provides a means to control baseline firing state without distorting the fine-scale temporal structure of sensory-evoked spike trains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sensory stimulation experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: All previous methods involving closed-loop or activity-guided optogenetic stimulation have used a physiological measurement to trigger static optical stimuli without corrective action or modification of stimulus parameters following stimulus onset.
source: All previous methods involving closed-loop or activity-guided optogenetic stimulation have used a physiological measurement to trigger static optical stimuli without corrective action or modification of stimulus parameters following stimulus onset (Leifer et al., 2011; Stirman et al., 2011; Paz et al., 2012; Krook-Magnuson et al., 2013; O'Connor et al., 2013; Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents the authors' assessment of the field.

claim: The optoclamp continuously updates stimulus intensity and frequency in real-time to enable precise control of neural firing in cultured networks and single cells in vivo.
source: In contrast, the optoclamp continuously updates stimulus intensity and frequency in real-time to enable precise control of neural firing in cultured networks and single cells in vivo and therefore provides a foundation for techniques aiming to achieved true closed-loop optical control of neural activity (Grosenick et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of the key finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout.

claim: The optoclamp provides a foundation for techniques aiming to achieve true closed-loop optical control of neural activity.
source: In contrast, the optoclamp continuously updates stimulus intensity and frequency in real-time to enable precise control of neural firing in cultured networks and single cells in vivo and therefore provides a foundation for techniques aiming to achieved true closed-loop optical control of neural activity (Grosenick et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation about the impact of the work, supported by citation to Grosenick et al., 2015.

claim: Even when using the same controller and target firing rate, successful control often required vastly different intensities of optical stimulation across experiments and experimental preparations.
source: Finally, we found that even when using the same controller and target firing rate, successful control often required vastly different intensities of optical stimulation across experiments and experimental preperations (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Closed-loop regulation of optical stimulation intensity may be a requirement, rather than a benefit, for evoking consistent activity levels across experiments.
source: This suggests that closed-loop regulation of optical stimulation intensity may be a requirment, rather than a benefit, for evoking consistent activity levels across experiments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of high variability in required stimulation intensity.
